sources.citation: Carr, Therese L. 2000. Wunambal: a language of the North-West Kimberley region, Western Australia. MA(Hons) thesis, University of New England. hdl 1959.11/16787. Section 2.4 Stress, pp.61-63.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: WUNAMBAL (closest described relative, not Miwa): 'In words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable'; 2-syllable words initial; 3-syllable mostly initial. Not applicable to miwa1242 first-hand.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1940. The classification of languages in North and North-West Australia. Oceania 10(3):241-272 (archive.org whole-issue scanned).
sources.note: Only a survey-wide remark (p.~243): 'Accent is also important, though it is difficult to set down rules for it.' Ba:gu (=Miwa/Bagu) appears only in noun-class and pronoun tables; classified as 'Drysdale: (ii) Galumburu-Bagu'.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page miwa1242 Miwa
sources.note: n/a; only references listed are Capell & Coate 1984 and Ethnologue 2025; 0 descriptive refs.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1939. The languages of the Northern Kimberley Division, W.A. Mankind 2(6): 169-175. DOI 10.1111/j.1835-9310.1939.tb00956.x
sources.note: No phonology beyond a transcription note (fn.1: modified IPA, 'A colon marks a long vowel'). Ba:gu content is grammatical only: 'In Gwi:ni there are five common Noun Classes; in Ba:gu there are the same number, but Wunambal has only three' (p.170-171); personal plural class 'not found in the other languages except Ba:gu'; 'In Gwi:ni and Ba:gu, Class I contains living persons, Class II..'; negative marking 'in Gwi:ni and Ba:gu' varies for tense (p.173); cave paintings 'found as far east as the Ba:gu tribe, but not amongst the Gwi:ni' (p.174). Nothing on accent/stress/tone.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul, Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2016. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 19th edition. Dallas: SIL International. Web entries 'Miwa [vmi]' (Internet Archive copy 2016-03-04) and 'Wunambal [wub]' (capture 2016-08-11); plus Grimes (ed.) 2000, 14th ed. web report 'WUB Wunambal' (capture 2005-02-21).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: no phonology content: vmi entry gives alt. name Bagu, 'No known L1 speakers', location Drysdale River, status 10 (Extinct), classification Australian > Worrorran, 'Language Development: Dictionary' (i.e. a dictionary exists -- cf. Coate ms / Gil 1934); the 19th-ed. wub entry and the 14th-ed. WUB web report have dialects/status/bilingualism only, the print typology line (index 0) is absent from the web versions read

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. & Alan Rumsey. 2009. Worrorran revisited: the case for genetic relations among languages of the Northern Kimberley region of Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 600. Canberra: ANU. hdl 1885/50063.
sources.note: Nothing for Miwa or any northern variety. Table 1 p.1: Miwa (Bagu, Miwi, Pela), 'a few speakers'; Table 2 p.4: 'Miwa -- Main sources of information: None'. Ch.4 phonology compares inventories of Worrorra, Ngarinyin, Gunin/Kwini, Wunambal only; sole stress mention is incidental (Unggumi mid vowels 'within initial stressed syllables').

sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Miwa entry has no structural content; Kwini entry refers to the Jawoyn entry (no prosody there)

sources.citation: McGregor, William. 1988. Handbook of Kimberley languages, vol. 1: General information. Pacific Linguistics C-105. Canberra: ANU. Entry 5.21 'Miwa / Bagu', pp.127-128.
sources.note: Nothing. Entry states: 'People who have worked intensively on the language: No one'; 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None'; word lists = Capell (1940), Coate unpublished 2,500-word dictionary, Lucich 400-600 words; AIATSIS K44.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur & H.H.J. Coate. 1984. Comparative studies in Northern Kimberley languages. Pacific Linguistics C-69. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C69.
sources.note: No stress section and no Miwa statement. pp.2,4-5: Forrest River people 'have variously been called Miwa, Yeidji, Gwini'; material treated under 'Gwini'/'Drysdale'. Only incidental stress remarks elsewhere: p.4 (Ngarinjin dialect forms) 'one of the very rare accents on a final syllable'; Worora kinship terms 'the fixity of the stress is noticeable'; pp.251-252 stress-conditioned auxiliary allomorphy in Wunambal/Worora.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1979. The history of Australian languages: a first approach. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), Australian Linguistic Studies, 419-619. Pacific Linguistics C-54. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C54.419.
sources.note: Gwini cited only for the initial cluster br-/gw- ('but this may be ber- (as in Gwini of Forrest River, Northern Kimberley)') and for dual/trial suffixes; nothing on stress or tone

sources.citation: Hernandez, T. 1941. Social organization of the Drysdale River tribes; Capell, A. 1941. Notes on the Wunambal language. Oceania 11(3) (archive.org whole-issue scanned).
sources.note: Nothing. Hernandez locates 'the Miwa tribe' from Buckle Head to Forrest River and notes Bagu is the name of the Drysdale mission site; ethnographic only.

sources.citation: Capell, A. & A. P. Elkin. 1937. The languages of the Kimberley Division. Oceania 8(2): 216-246. DOI 10.1002/j.1834-4461.1937.tb00417.x
sources.note: Only a list of phonetic symbols (p.216 fn.); no accent/stress remarks for any Northern Kimberley language. Forrest River appears only in pronoun tables (pp.233-234) and in the remark 'it is doubly unfortunate that the Forrest River languages have not been investigated' (p.233).
